title: Level 1 – Cyber Starter (Year 7)
_about: Written by Anish Shrestha (2) and Kiri Rāwiri (simulated). Draft for Cultural Guide review. Every question: 5 marks. Categories: CB, ETH, PWD, PRIV.

questions.text: What does "cybersecurity" mean?

options.A: Protecting devices, accounts and information from harm

questions.feedback: Cybersecurity protects our devices, accounts and information from people or programs that want to harm, steal or trick us.

questions.text: What is malware?

options.C: A program made to harm a device or steal information

questions.feedback: "Malware" means malicious software, such as viruses and spyware.

questions.text: Why should you install software updates?

options.D: They fix security holes and bugs

questions.feedback: Updates close the gaps that attackers use, so keep your device and apps up to date.

questions.scenario_text: You are doing homework when a big red pop-up appears: "WARNING! Your device has 5 viruses! Click here NOW to clean it!"
questions.text: What should you do?

options.A: Click quickly before the viruses spread
options.B: Close the page and tell a trusted adult
options.C: Type your password to fix it

questions.feedback: Scary pop-ups try to rush you into clicking. Stop, close it, and ask a trusted adult.

questions.text: True or false: most cyber attacks start by tricking a person.
questions.feedback: Many attacks use tricks (social engineering), so good habits are your best defence.

questions.scenario_text: A text message says: "NZ Post: your parcel is waiting. Pay a $2.99 delivery fee here: nzpost-delivery-fee.info". Nobody in your family ordered anything.
questions.text: What is the safest thing to do?

options.A: Pay the $2.99 because it is cheap
options.B: Click the link to see what the parcel is
options.D: Do not click; show a trusted adult and delete it

questions.feedback: Fake delivery messages are a very common scam in New Zealand. Do not click or reply – show an adult and delete it.

questions.scenario_text: Your friend forgot to log out of a school computer in the library.
questions.text: What is the right thing to do?

options.A: Log them out or tell them

questions.feedback: Using someone else's account is not okay, even as a joke. Logging them out protects them.

questions.text: Is it okay to post a photo of a classmate online without asking?

options.D: Yes, if your account is private

questions.feedback: Everyone has the right to decide about their own photo. Always ask first.

questions.text: Copying someone's work and saying it is yours is called…
questions.feedback: Plagiarism is not fair to the person who did the work. Always give credit.

questions.scenario_text: In a group chat, some students keep sending mean messages about one classmate.
questions.text: What is the best action?

options.A: Don't join in, keep a screenshot and tell a trusted adult
options.C: Join in so they do not pick on you

questions.feedback: Tell a teacher or whānau member. Netsafe can also help with online bullying.

questions.text: What does "think before you post" mean?

options.B: Post as fast as you can
options.D: Posts can stay online for a long time and affect you and others

questions.feedback: Your digital footprint can last for years, so post things you will still be happy with later.

questions.text: Which of these are ethical (right) things to do online? Choose ALL that apply.

options.A: Ask before sharing a friend's photo
options.B: Give credit to the artist when you use their picture
options.C: Log in to a friend's game account without asking
options.D: Report a hurtful post to a trusted adult

questions.feedback: Asking permission, giving credit and reporting harm are all ethical. Using someone's account without asking is not.

questions.text: True or false: "anish123" is a strong password.
questions.feedback: A name plus simple numbers is easy to guess. Use a long passphrase instead.

questions.text: Which of these is the strongest password?
questions.feedback: Long passphrases with different kinds of characters are very hard to guess.

questions.text: Should you use the same password for every account?

options.A: Yes, it is easier to remember
options.B: No, use a different password for each important account

questions.feedback: If one account is hacked, the others stay safe when each password is different.

questions.scenario_text: Your best friend says: "Tell me your game password so I can level up your character while you are away."
questions.text: What should you do?

options.A: Share it because they are your best friend
options.D: Post it in the group chat

questions.feedback: Passwords are private, even from friends. A parent or caregiver can help you manage them.

questions.text: What is two-step verification (MFA)?

options.A: An extra check, like a code from an app, after your password
options.D: Sharing your password with two people

questions.feedback: Even if someone steals your password, they still need the second step to log in.

questions.text: Which of these make a password stronger? Choose ALL that apply.

options.A: Making it long (12 or more characters)

questions.feedback: Length, random words and a mix of characters make passwords strong. Birthdays are easy to find and guess.

questions.scenario_text: A player in a game chat says: "You're really good! What school do you go to and how old are you?"
questions.text: What should you do?

options.C: Send a photo of your uniform
options.D: Don't share it and tell a trusted adult

questions.feedback: Strangers online may not be who they say they are. Keep personal details private.

questions.text: A message says "You won a free phone! Send your home address." What is it most likely to be?
questions.feedback: If it sounds too good to be true, it probably is a scam. Don't reply; tell an adult.

questions.text: Which is safest to share on a public profile?
questions.feedback: Share hobbies, not details that show where you are or how to contact you.

questions.text: Someone you met online wants to meet you in person. What should you do?

options.C: Tell a trusted adult and never meet alone

questions.feedback: A trusted adult can check if it is safe. Never meet an online-only friend alone.

questions.text: Who can help in New Zealand if something online makes you feel unsafe?

options.D: A trusted adult (teacher, whānau) and Netsafe

questions.feedback: You are never alone – talk to a trusted adult, and Netsafe can help too.

questions.text: Which of these are personal information you should keep private online? Choose ALL that apply.
questions.feedback: Address, password and phone number can be used to find or trick you. Your favourite colour is fine to share.
